title: Fusion power: what the recent records do and do not mean
hook: A record laser shot, a plasma held for 22 minutes, the most fusion energy ever. All true. Three questions show how far a power plant still is.

lines.text: Every few months, there is a new headline about fusion. A record energy yield from a laser. A plasma held for twenty-two minutes. The most fusion energy ever made in one go.
Each of these records is real.
And yet none of them means that a fusion power plant is around the corner. They measure very different things.
Today you get a small tool: three questions for any fusion headline.

scenes.title: What has to happen
scenes.svg:

</g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">

</g>

lines.text: Fusion means that two light atomic nuclei merge into a heavier one. A tiny part of their mass turns into a lot of energy.
The best fuel is a pair of heavy types of hydrogen: deuterium and tritium. They merge into helium and a fast neutron.
The problem: both nuclei carry a positive charge, so they push each other away.
To get past that push, they must collide at enormous speed. And for particles, speed means temperature.
On Earth, that takes about 150 million degrees. At that heat, matter is a plasma: a gas of loose, charged particles.

scenes.title: Three numbers at once
scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="42" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up">three things, at the same moment</text>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up"><rect x="24" y="64" width="104" height="104" rx="14" class="fp"/><text x="76" y="114" class="mid tl tb fc">hot</text><text x="76" y="142" class="mid ts fm">fast collisions</text></g>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up" data-d="4"><rect x="148" y="64" width="104" height="104" rx="14" class="fp"/><text x="200" y="114" class="mid tl tb fa">dense</text><text x="200" y="142" class="mid ts fm">many collisions</text><text x="138" y="122" class="mid tm fm">×</text></g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up"><rect x="272" y="64" width="104" height="104" rx="14" class="fp"/><text x="324" y="114" class="mid tl tb fd">long</text><text x="324" y="142" class="mid ts fm">heat stays in</text><text x="262" y="122" class="mid tm fm">×</text></g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<text x="200" y="212" class="mid tl tb fb">= the triple product</text>
<text x="200" y="236" class="mid ts fm">the real scoreboard of fusion research</text>
</g>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<text x="200" y="286" class="mid ts fm">like lighting damp wood:</text>
<text x="200" y="308" class="mid ts">enough heat, on enough wood, for long enough</text>
<text x="200" y="340" class="mid ts fb tb">until the fire feeds itself</text>
</g>

lines.text: Heat alone is not enough. Three things must be right at the same moment.
The fuel must be hot enough, so that a collision can end in fusion. And dense enough, so that there are many collisions.
And the heat must stay inside long enough, before it leaks away. This holding is called confinement.
Multiply the three numbers, and you get the triple product. It is the real scoreboard of fusion research.
Think of lighting damp wood. You need enough heat, on enough wood, for long enough, until the fire feeds itself.

lines.text: No material can touch a plasma at a hundred million degrees. So there are two main ways to hold it.
The first way uses magnets. The plasma is charged, so a magnetic field can steer it. The usual machine bends it into a ring and is called a tokamak.
Here the fuel is far thinner than air. So it has to be held for a long time: seconds, or better, minutes.
The second way does the opposite. Lasers crush a tiny pellet of fuel so hard that it becomes denser than lead. Then a billionth of a second is long enough.
One way bets on time, the other on density. So their records look very different.

lines.text: Record number one comes from the laser side, from the National Ignition Facility in California.
192 laser beams hit a capsule the size of a peppercorn. In December 2022, for the first time, more fusion energy came out than laser energy went in.
In April 2025, the record rose to 8.6 megajoules, from about 2 megajoules of laser light. That is a gain of roughly 4.
The fuel reached ignition: the fusion reactions heated the fuel themselves, which set off even more reactions.
For sixty years, nobody knew whether that could be done in a laboratory at all. Now we know.

scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="40" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up">energy out, compared with which energy in?</text>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up">
<text x="24" y="126" class="ts fc">laser light onto the capsule: 2 MJ</text><rect x="24" y="134" width="3" height="14" rx="1" class="fc"/>
<text x="24" y="176" class="ts fd">fusion energy out: 8.6 MJ</text><rect x="24" y="184" width="10" height="14" rx="2" class="fd"/>
</g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<text x="24" y="76" class="ts">drawn from the grid: about 300 MJ</text><rect x="24" y="84" width="352" height="14" rx="4" class="fm"/>
</g>
<text x="200" y="232" class="mid tm tb fc" data-l="3" data-fx="up">back: about 3% of what went in</text>
<text x="200" y="266" class="mid ts" data-l="4" data-fx="up">8.6 MJ would boil about 25 litres of water</text>
<g data-l="5" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="292" width="170" height="60" rx="12" class="fp"/><text x="109" y="316" class="mid ts fm">today</text><text x="109" y="338" class="mid ts tb">about 1 shot a day</text>
</g>
<g data-l="5" data-fx="up" data-d="4">
<rect x="206" y="292" width="170" height="60" rx="12" class="fp sc"/><text x="291" y="316" class="mid ts fm">a power plant</text><text x="291" y="338" class="mid ts tb fc">about 10 per second</text>
</g>

lines.text: Now the first of our three questions: energy out, compared with which energy in?
The gain of 4 compares the fusion energy with the laser light that hit the capsule.
But the lasers themselves are wasteful. To deliver those 2 megajoules, they draw roughly 300 megajoules from the grid.
Measured against that, the shot gave back about three percent.
And the amount is small: enough to bring about 25 litres of water to the boil.
The laboratory fires such a shot about once a day at most. A power plant would need around ten every second, each with a fresh capsule.

lines.text: So the word gain can mean very different things. The physics gain compares the fusion energy with the energy that was put into the fuel.
The plant gain compares electricity out with electricity in. It includes every loss: the wasteful lasers or heaters at the start, and the turbine at the end.
A turbine alone turns only about forty percent of the heat into electricity.
As far as public results show, no fusion machine has reached a plant gain above one. None has fed electricity into a grid.
A rule of thumb: for a plant, the physics gain must be far above one. With magnets, ten or more. With lasers, fifty or more.

quiz.q: A laser shot draws 400 MJ from the grid. 2 MJ reach the fuel, 10 MJ of fusion heat come out. A turbine turns 40% of heat into power. What is the plant gain?

options.text: 0.025: two and a half percent comes back
options.why: That compares the 10 megajoules of heat with the 400 from the grid. But heat is not electricity yet. The turbine keeps only 40 percent of it, so 4.

options.text: 2: twice the energy that went into the fuel
options.why: The 4 megajoules of electricity are right. But the plant gain compares them with all the electricity the plant drew, 400, not with the 2 that reached the fuel.

options.text: 5: five times the energy that went into the fuel
options.why: That is the physics gain: 10 out for 2 into the fuel. The plant gain also counts the wasteful lasers before and the turbine after.

options.text: 0.01: one percent of the electricity comes back
options.why: The turbine makes 4 megajoules of electricity out of the 10 megajoules of heat. Compared with the 400 that were drawn from the grid, that is one hundredth.

quiz.explain: Picture a food stall. You hand the cook ingredients worth 2 euros, and the dish he makes is worth 10. Five times the value: that is the physics gain. But you are the owner. To get those ingredients onto his table, you paid 400 euros for rent, staff and power. And the customer does not pay 10 for the dish. After all the losses, 4 euros reach your till. So you spent 400 and got 4 back, which is one hundredth. That is the plant gain. Both numbers are honest. They just answer different questions. A headline almost always quotes the first one. A power company only cares about the second.

scenes.title: Record two: the long plasma
scenes.svg:
<g data-l="0" data-fx="up">
<text x="200" y="40" class="mid ts fm">WEST tokamak, France, February 2025</text>
<text x="200" y="92" class="mid tx tb fa">22 minutes</text>
<rect x="24" y="110" width="352" height="16" rx="8" class="fa"/>
</g>
<text x="200" y="152" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up" data-d="6">1,337 seconds</text>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="pop" data-d="0.6"><rect x="24" y="184" width="110" height="34" rx="10" class="fp"/><text x="79" y="206" class="mid ts ">plain hydrogen</text></g><g data-l="1" data-fx="pop" data-d="1.7999999999999998"><rect x="140" y="184" width="104" height="34" rx="10" class="fp"/><text x="192" y="206" class="mid ts ">50 million °C</text></g><g data-l="1" data-fx="pop" data-d="3"><rect x="250" y="184" width="126" height="34" rx="10" class="fp"/><text x="313" y="206" class="mid ts ">≈ no fusion energy</text></g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<text x="200" y="262" class="mid tm tb fb">what was tested: endurance</text>
<text x="200" y="288" class="mid ts fm">walls, heating and control, without a break</text>
</g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="316" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="343" class="mid ts">one number pushed far, two still low</text>
</g>

lines.text: Record number two comes from the magnet side. In February 2025, a French tokamak called WEST held a plasma for 1,337 seconds. That is 22 minutes.
Here comes our second question: was it real fuel, or a stand-in? It was plain hydrogen, at about fifty million degrees. That gives almost no fusion energy.
So what was tested? Endurance. Can the walls, the heating and the control systems run that long without a break?
That is a necessary step, because a plant must run for days. But it is one of the three numbers pushed far, while the other two stay low.

quiz.q: A tokamak held a plain hydrogen plasma at about 50 million degrees for 22 minutes. What does this record show most directly?

options.text: That the triple product for a power plant was reached
options.why: Time is only one of the three numbers. Temperature and density were well below what a plant needs, so the product stays far too low.

options.text: That the machine made fusion energy for 22 minutes
options.why: Plain hydrogen at 50 million degrees hardly fuses at all. The plasma was hot and stable, but it was not a fire. It was held hot from outside.

options.text: That magnets beat lasers, whose shots last an instant
options.why: The two ways cannot be compared by time. Lasers work with extreme density and need only an instant. Magnets work with thin fuel and need long times.

options.text: That walls, heating and control survive a long run
options.why: With plain hydrogen at this temperature there is almost no fusion. What ran for 22 minutes was the machine itself: its walls, its heating, its control.

quiz.explain: Imagine a team that wants to build an engine for a flight around the world. One day they report: our engine ran for 22 minutes without a break. Then you learn that it ran without load, on a test stand, turned by an electric motor from outside, and with water in the tank instead of fuel. Was the test useless? Not at all. Bearings, cooling and control held for 22 minutes, and before that they failed after seconds. But the test says nothing about power, and nothing about the fuel. The long plasma is that kind of test. It checks the endurance of the machine, not the fusion.

<text x="200" y="94" class="mid tx tb fd">69 MJ</text>
<text x="200" y="118" class="mid ts fm">of fusion energy, in 5 seconds</text>
</g>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="140" width="352" height="64" rx="14" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="166" class="mid ts tb">real fuel: deuterium + tritium</text>
<text x="200" y="188" class="mid ts fm">only 0.2 milligrams of it</text>
</g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<text x="24" y="242" class="ts">heating in</text><rect x="116" y="229" width="240" height="16" rx="5" class="fc"/>
<text x="24" y="272" class="ts">fusion out</text><rect x="116" y="259" width="80" height="16" rx="5" class="fd"/>
<text x="200" y="310" class="mid ts fc tb">physics gain: well below 1</text>
</g>
<text x="200" y="350" class="mid ts fm" data-l="3" data-fx="up">built in the 1980s, too small for more, now closed</text>

lines.text: Record number three: the most fusion energy from a magnetic machine. In late 2023, the European tokamak JET made 69 megajoules in 5 seconds.
This time it was the real fuel, deuterium and tritium, and only 0.2 milligrams of it.
But the heating used roughly three times more energy than the fusion gave back. The physics gain was well below one.
JET was built in the 1980s and was too small to do better. After this run, it was shut down.

lines.text: Put the three records side by side.
The laser shot had real fuel and a physics gain above one. But it lasts an instant, about once a day.
The long plasma ran for twenty-two minutes, but without real fuel, and without any gain.
The energy record had real fuel, but no gain, and it lasted five seconds.
Each record ticks one or two boxes. A power plant has to tick all of them, in one machine, all day long. And the last box, electricity, is empty for everyone.

lines.text: And there are boxes that no record has touched. The first is the wall.
Four fifths of the fusion energy leave the plasma as fast neutrons. Neutrons carry no charge, so the magnetic field cannot hold them.
They fly straight into the wall. That is how the heat gets out. But each neutron also knocks atoms in the metal out of place.
Over the years, every atom in the wall is hit many times. The metal swells, turns brittle and becomes radioactive.
No material has been tested under this load for long, because no machine can produce it yet.

lines.text: The second open box is the fuel. Deuterium comes from seawater. Tritium is the problem.
Tritium hardly exists in nature, because it decays. Half of any amount is gone after twelve years.
The whole world holds only a few tens of kilograms, a by-product of one type of nuclear reactor.
One large fusion plant would burn more than fifty kilograms a year.
So every plant must make its own. The wall is wrapped in a layer with lithium. When a neutron hits lithium, new tritium is born.
The plant must breed a little more than one new atom for each atom it burns. That has never been shown in a full machine.

quiz.q: A plant breeds 0.95 new tritium atoms for each one it burns. Other reactors supply only a few kilograms a year worldwide. What follows?

options.text: It can run on deuterium alone at the same temperature instead
options.why: Deuterium alone fuses far less easily. It would need a much higher triple product, which no machine is close to. Tritium is used because it is the easy case.

options.text: It is almost self-sufficient, so the small gap is easy to buy
options.why: Five percent of more than 50 kilograms is over two and a half kilograms a year, for a single plant. That is about what the whole world makes.

options.text: Its stock shrinks, and a fleet of such plants cannot run
options.why: Below one, the plant uses up more than it makes. The outside supply is tiny, so one plant might be kept alive, but never hundreds of them.

options.text: It can stockpile the missing tritium before it starts up
options.why: A stock does not keep. Half of it is gone after twelve years. And there is nothing to stock up from: the world holds only a few tens of kilograms.

quiz.explain: Think of a baker who makes sourdough bread. Every day he keeps back a piece of dough as the starter for the next day. Now suppose he always keeps back five percent too little. For a while nobody notices. But the starter gets smaller every single day, and one day there is not enough left to bake. Could he buy more? In this town nobody sells starter, apart from one neighbour who can spare a spoonful a year. Could he fill the cellar with it in advance? It spoils. A fusion plant is in the same position. Tritium cannot be bought in quantity and cannot be stored for long. So a ratio just below one is not almost good enough. It is a plant that slowly runs dry.

lines.text: So why all the new optimism, and the private money? One reason is a real technical jump: better magnets.
Newer superconductors can carry far more current. In 2021, a team near Boston built a large magnet with a field of 20 tesla. The magnets of the giant ITER machine reach about 12.
This matters because of a steep rule. The fusion power you get from a given volume rises with the fourth power of the field.
Double the field, and the same volume gives sixteen times the power. So a machine can be much smaller.
Smaller means cheaper and faster to build. That is what made fusion something that start-ups dare to try.

No electricity, ever</text></g>

lines.text: The big public project is ITER, in France. Its goal: a physics gain of 10, which means 500 megawatts of fusion from 50 of heating.
Its start has been pushed to 2034, and real fuel to 2039. And it will never make electricity. It is an experiment.
The best-known private machine, SPARC, uses the new magnets. It has about a fortieth of the volume, is planned to start in 2027, and aims at a gain above 1.
Another company, Helion, has a contract to supply Microsoft from 2028. Reports from this autumn say that full power is not expected before 2029 or 2030.
Note the pattern. These are plans, and fusion dates have almost always slipped.

<text x="86" y="94" class="ts fm">no real fuel: no real fusion energy</text>
</g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="122" width="352" height="70" rx="14" class="fp"/>

<text x="86" y="174" class="ts fm">into the fuel, or from the socket?</text>
</g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="202" width="352" height="70" rx="14" class="fp"/>

</g>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<text x="200" y="312" class="mid ts">no answer to any of the three?</text>
<text x="200" y="340" class="mid tm tb fc">then it is about hope, not results</text>
</g>

lines.text: Now you have the tool. When the next fusion headline comes, ask three questions.
One: was it real fuel, or a stand-in such as plain hydrogen? Without real fuel, there is no real fusion energy.
Two: energy out, compared with which energy in? Into the fuel, or from the wall socket? The two can differ by a factor of a hundred.
Three: how long, and how often? An instant once a day is a physics result. A power plant means all day, every day.
If an article answers none of the three, it is telling you about hope, not about results.

quiz.q: A company reports: plasma at 100 million degrees, held for a hundredth of a second, in plain hydrogen. No energy figures. What is the fairest reading?

options.text: It is worthless, because no fusion energy was measured
options.why: That is too harsh. Without this temperature nothing else can follow, and reaching it in a new machine is real progress. It is a step, not a result.

options.text: One of three conditions is shown; gain is still open
options.why: The temperature is a real and necessary step. But the holding time is very short, the fuel was a stand-in, and nothing is said about energy.

options.text: It is close to a plant: only the fuel has to be swapped now
options.why: Swapping the fuel is the hard part. Real fuel brings fast neutrons, wall damage and the tritium problem. And the holding time is still far too short.

options.text: Fusion works there, because that is hotter than the sun
options.why: The sun is a poor yardstick. It gets by with less heat because gravity holds its fuel for billions of years. On Earth, heat is only one of three numbers.

quiz.explain: Use the three questions one after the other. Real fuel? No, plain hydrogen, so there was no real fusion energy, no neutrons and no fuel cycle. Energy out against which energy in? The report gives no number at all, which usually means there is nothing to show yet. How long and how often? A hundredth of a second. So what is left is one true thing: the machine can reach the needed temperature. That is like a new restaurant reporting that its oven reaches 250 degrees. Good, and necessary. But nobody has cooked a meal yet, and nobody knows whether the kitchen can serve two hundred guests a night.

<g data-l="1" data-fx="up"><rect x="24" y="216" width="112" height="106" rx="12" class="fp sa"/><text x="80" y="242" class="mid ts fm">next few years</text><text x="80" y="266" class="mid ts tb fa">gain above 1</text><text x="80" y="284" class="mid ts tb fa">with magnets</text></g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up"><rect x="144" y="150" width="112" height="172" rx="12" class="fp sb"/><text x="200" y="176" class="mid ts fm">the 2030s</text><text x="200" y="200" class="mid ts tb fb">first power</text><text x="200" y="218" class="mid ts tb fb">into a grid</text></g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up"><rect x="264" y="84" width="112" height="238" rx="12" class="fp sd"/><text x="320" y="110" class="mid ts fm">after 2050</text><text x="320" y="134" class="mid ts tb fd">a real share</text><text x="320" y="152" class="mid ts tb fd">of world power</text></g>
<text x="200" y="350" class="mid ts" data-l="4" data-fx="up">too late for the climate goals of the next 20 years</text>
<text x="200" y="374" class="mid ts fd tb" data-l="5" data-fx="up">as a long bet: more serious than ever</text>

lines.text: So what is a fair expectation? Take this as an estimate, not as a fact.
A magnetic machine with a physics gain above one in the next few years is plausible. That will make headlines.
First pilot plants that feed some electricity into a grid may follow in the twenty thirties, if the wall and the fuel are solved in time.
A real share of the world's electricity is something for the second half of this century.
So fusion comes too late for the climate goals of the next twenty years. Those need what already works: sun, wind and storage.
But as a bet on the long run, it has never looked more serious than now.

lines.text: The short version. Fusion needs fuel that is hot enough, dense enough, and held long enough, all at once.
The recent records are real, but each ticks only one or two boxes.
Nobody has ticked the hard engineering boxes: a wall that survives, fuel bred inside the plant, and electricity at the end.
Stronger magnets made the machines smaller and brought in private money. That speeds things up, but the open boxes remain.
Tomorrow we turn to business: pricing, and why most small companies charge too little.

takeaways: Fusion needs three things at once: fuel that is hot enough, dense enough, and held long enough. Their product is the real scoreboard.
The laser record (8.6 MJ, gain about 4) proved ignition. But measured against the electricity the lasers drew, about 3% came back.
Physics gain compares fusion energy with the energy put into the fuel. Plant gain compares electricity out with electricity in. No machine has a plant gain above 1.
The 22-minute plasma used plain hydrogen: a test of endurance, not of fusion. The 69 MJ record used real fuel, but with a gain well below 1.
Two problems are untouched by any record: walls that survive fast neutrons, and tritium, which each plant has to breed for itself.
Three questions for any headline: Real fuel or a stand-in? Energy out compared with which energy in? How long, and how often?
